passages.text: The nature of the one and only God, who made the world, created us, and provided everything, is naturally such that, in the case of anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit, it carries that person’s soul toward him by affection for him, in the form of an innate longing for him. Even if that person is a sinner, after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved. If someone denies him or in some other way speaks impiously against him, then repents, he will indeed be punished for the ways in which he sinned against him, but he will be saved, because after turning back he loved him. Perhaps, however, if there is an extraordinary degree of reverence and supplication, he will even be released from punishment, having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin. Those, however, who have not repented will also meet their end through the punishment of fire, even if they are most devout in every other respect. But, as I said, after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age, they will be extinguished. For those who have acted impiously against the eternal and only God can no longer exist forever.

lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the repeated nature language of πέφυκεν and φύσις while allowing the following infinitive to express what this nature characteristically does.
Preserves the possessive expression and descriptive wording without using English capitalization to settle personhood beyond what the Greek itself marks.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ τὸ κατ’ ἀξίαν ὧν ἔπραξεν κολασθῆναι σώζεσθαι φύσιν ἔχει
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished as his deeds deserve, it is in his nature to be saved
lexical_decisions.rationale: κατ’ ἀξίαν expresses punishment corresponding to the worth or deserts of the deeds, while φύσιν ἔχει continues the passage’s emphasis on nature.

The response follows denial or impious speech and precedes the stated turning back and love, supporting moral-spiritual repentance under the October13 contextual policy. The later noun and negated participle receive the same cognate repentance terminology. The distinct ἐπιστρέψας remains after turning back rather than being merged with repent. No destination or intensifier is added, and the historical author's stated punishment-and-salvation framework is left intact.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: συγγνώμης τῆς ἁμαρτίας μετὰ τῆς μετανοίας δεδωκὼς τὴν ἄγνοιαν
lexical_decisions.chosen: having presented his ignorance together with his repentance as grounds for forgiveness of the sin
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact construction presents ignorance and repentance in relation to pardon. It may alternatively be understood as offering ignorance as an excuse for the sin, but the chosen wording preserves both elements without making ignorance itself absolve him. Repentance reflects the morally responsive context rather than a mere change of opinion; no new condition or causal formula is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μεμετρημένου αἰῶνος τὸ πέμπτον πυρὶ αἰωνίῳ κολασθέντες
lexical_decisions.chosen: after being punished with age-long fire for one fifth of a measured age
lexical_decisions.rationale: “Age-long” preserves the relation between αἰωνίῳ and αἰῶνος and fits the explicitly measured duration. “Eternal fire” is a possible lexical alternative, in which case the fire rather than each person’s punishment would be described as eternal.
Preserves the image of something being put out rather than replacing it with an interpretive abstraction such as “annihilated.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος καὶ μὴ βλασφημοῦντος αὐτοῦ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the case of anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God and does not blaspheme his holy spirit
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied smooth-breathed negative adverb is retained as never, with substantival παντός and participle ὄντος forming a genitive absolute. The coordinated nonblasphemy is also retained. The positive indefinite οὑδήποτε would be a different proposed reading, not a meaning licensed by this supplied negative form; it appears only as an explicitly hypothetical alternative in the source note. The contextual difficulty is not resolved by deleting or reversing the negative or adding a new theological condition.

source_issues.source_quote: παντὸς οὐδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος
source_issues.issue: The selected confirmed print has smooth-breathed οὐδήποτε, ordinarily never, and that negative is translated in the main text. Substantival παντός supplies the person in a genitive absolute, while never modifies ὄντος: anyone who is never within the bounds of reverence for God. This is syntactically defensible, although the qualification is contextually difficult beside coordinated nonblasphemy and innate longing for God. A distinctly hypothetical contextual correction changes the breathing to genitive indefinite οὑδήποτε, of anyone whatsoever, producing a positive qualification such as anyone whatsoever who is within the bounds. That proposal would change the negative meaning and is not the supplied Greek or the main translation. It remains only a labeled alternative; no source alteration, newly verified corrected wording, or unique original recovery is claimed.
source_issues.proposed_reading: παντὸς οὑδήποτε ἐντὸς ὅρων θεοσεβείας ὄντος

source_issues.issue: The confirmed printed raised dot interrupts the natural construction in which ἰδέᾳ governs the preceding genitive phrase. Treating it as sentence-final would leave ἰδέᾳ isolated before the full stop. The translation therefore provisionally treats the raised dot as anomalous internal editorial punctuation and attaches ἰδέᾳ to the preceding words.
